newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi, Ciampi play down deficit figures.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi, Ciampi play down deficit figures.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi have played down larger-than-expected 1996 deficit figures released on Friday, saying the shortfall did not reflect actual state finances.
"The data are absolutely under control. There is nothing new here and there is nothing to worry about," Prodi was quoted on Saturday as saying in most major newspapers.

His comments followed the Treasury's announcement on Friday that Italy had run up a 1996 public sector deficit of 138.50 trillion lire ($90.5 billion) -- well ahead of a revised government target of 123 trillion lire.

Ciampi also played down the figures, saying they were swollen by local authorities drawing heavily on their accounts with the Treasury in the closing weeks of 1996 in anticipation of a tight squeeze on spending in the year just begun.
"The overall deficit for 1996 compared to forecasts was due to the performance of Treasury accounts and not to a shortfall in the state budget," Ciampi said in a statement released late on Friday.
"The overall performance of state finances stayed in line with what was forecast; thus there is no reason to fear any consequences on the figures for 1997," he added.

Economists have said the 1996 deficit figures mean Italy faces a monumental task in 1997 to bring its public finances to heel and secure a berth in European economic and monetary union (EMU) ahead of its launch in two years' time.

The government will decide early in 1997 whether to bite the fiscal bullet even harder by passing more belt-tightening measures after parliament already approved a 62.5 trillion lire deficit-cutting package at the end of the year. ($1=1,536 lire) --Rome newsroom 396 678 2505
